name: Breathing Water  -  How Gills Pull Oxygen from the Sea
scope: The spine is the gill as an oxygen-extraction machine. Rungs: water carries far less oxygen than air, so a fish must pass a huge volume over its gills; water enters the mouth and exits under the operculum (gill cover) in a one-way flow; the gill filaments split into tiny lamellae stacked to make enormous surface area; blood flows through the lamellae in the OPPOSITE direction to the water (countercurrent exchange) so oxygen keeps diffusing across the whole length; a tuna or mackerel can't work its gill cover fast enough at speed, so it swims mouth-open to ram water through (ram ventilation) and dies if it stops; sharks likewise — most must keep moving, though nurse sharks pump water while resting on the bottom; the axolotl and mudpuppy keep feathery EXTERNAL gills for life. Payoff rung: countercurrent flow lets a fish strip up to ~80% of the water's oxygen, far more than a simple side-by-side flow could.
source: Britannica; FishBase; Kardong Vertebrates textbook
framing_note: Scene-led: a harvested fish's gills are the concrete handle — red feathery stacks under the flap. The wonder is countercurrent exchange (blood and water running opposite ways), and the ram-ventilator that drowns if it stops swimming. T1 base: recognize gills = underwater breathing organ. Real terms (operculum, lamellae, countercurrent) introduced with the concrete image, never as bare definitions. No anthropomorphizing.

name: Air-Breathers in Water  -  Lungs Where You'd Expect Gills
scope: The spine is animals in water that still breathe AIR, and the tricks that let them. Rungs: whales and dolphins are mammals with lungs, not gills — they surface to breathe through a blowhole (nostrils moved to the top of the head) and hold their breath while diving; the lungfish (Protopterus, Lepidosiren) gulps air into a true lung and can survive a dried-up pool by burrowing into mud and sealing itself in a mucus cocoon (aestivation) for months; the diving beetle carries a shining silver bubble of air trapped under its wing covers, using it like a scuba tank and even drawing extra oxygen from the water into the bubble (a physical gill); the water spider builds a diving-bell of silk and fills it with air; the electric eel and the betta breathe air at the surface with a special organ; sea snakes and marine iguanas hold their breath and dive on a single lungful. Payoff rung: the diving-beetle bubble is a 'physical gill' — as the beetle uses up oxygen, more oxygen diffuses IN from the surrounding water, refilling the bubble.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; entomology & ichthyology refs
framing_note: Scene-led wonder: the SILVER bubble under a beetle's wings, the lungfish waking from months buried in dry mud. Named animals anchor each rung. Keep the physics of the bubble-gill accurate (diffusion refill, but nitrogen eventually forces a resurface). Whale blowhole = nostrils relocated, stated plainly. No anthropomorphizing.

name: Why Insects Can't Be Giant  -  The Tracheae Problem
scope: The spine is the insect's air-tube breathing system and the size ceiling it imposes. Rungs: insects have no lungs and no blood-borne oxygen delivery — instead air enters through holes along the body called spiracles and runs through branching tubes (tracheae) that carry oxygen DIRECTLY to every cell; this works beautifully for small bodies but the tubes rely mostly on diffusion, which fails over long distances, so a big insect's core would suffocate; that physics caps insect size; in the Carboniferous, ~300 million years ago, the atmosphere held far more oxygen (~30% vs today's 21%), and giant insects lived then — Meganeura, a dragonfly-relative with a ~70 cm wingspan, and Arthropleura, a millipede-relative over 2 m long; when oxygen fell, the giants vanished; some large insects actively pump their abdomens to push air through the tubes. Payoff rung: the reason a beetle the size of a dog can't exist is not its shell but its plumbing — diffusion can't feed a large insect's core.
source: Britannica; Smithsonian; paleoclimate & entomology literature
framing_note: Wonder hook is the Carboniferous giants (Meganeura, Arthropleura) and WHY they were possible then but not now — the answer is the tracheal/oxygen limit. Numbers (30% O2, 70 cm wingspan) only where the stem constructs the contrast. Spiracles/tracheae taught via the image of air-holes and tubes, not bare terms. Flag that exact O2 percentages are estimated from proxies.

name: Extraordinary Hearts & Blood
scope: The spine is unusual circulatory solutions across animals. Rungs: the octopus has THREE hearts — two branchial hearts pump blood through the gills, one systemic heart drives it round the body — and its blood is BLUE because it carries oxygen with copper-based hemocyanin, not iron-based hemoglobin; the systemic heart stops when the octopus swims, which is why it prefers to crawl; the giraffe faces a blood-pressure problem — pumping blood up a 2 m neck to the brain needs roughly double a human's pressure, driven by a huge thick-walled heart, and tight skin plus special valves stop the blood rushing to its head when it bends down to drink; the horseshoe crab also has blue copper blood, prized by medicine for detecting contamination; the icefish of Antarctic waters has clear, nearly colorless blood with almost NO oxygen-carrying pigment, relying on cold, oxygen-rich water and a huge heart; the earthworm has several simple 'hearts' (aortic arches). Payoff rung: octopus and horseshoe-crab blood is blue because copper, not iron, ferries the oxygen.
source: Britannica; Marine Biological Laboratory; comparative physiology refs
framing_note: Named-thing wonders: three hearts, blue copper blood, the giraffe's supercharged heart-and-valve system. Each rung one coherent fact. Keep hemocyanin/hemoglobin accurate (copper vs iron). Giraffe blood-pressure figures only as a constructed contrast with human. Icefish is the no-pigment payoff — flag it as a genuine oddity. No anthropomorphizing.

name: Growing It Back  -  Regeneration
scope: The spine is regrowing lost body parts, ranked from partial to jaw-dropping. Rungs: a starfish can regrow a lost arm, and in some species a single severed arm with part of the central disc can grow into a whole new starfish; a lizard drops its tail to escape and regrows it, but the replacement is cartilage, not true bone; the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) regrows entire limbs, its tail, parts of its heart, and even portions of its brain and spinal cord — perfectly, without scarring — which is why labs study it; the planarian flatworm is the champion — cut it into pieces and each piece can regrow into a complete worm, head and all, using a reserve of stem cells (neoblasts); the sea cucumber can regrow expelled internal organs; a deer regrows an entire set of antlers every year, the fastest bone growth known in mammals. Payoff rung: cut a planarian into fragments and each fragment builds a whole new worm — a two-headed worm can even be made in the lab.
source: Britannica; regeneration literature; axolotl research reviews
framing_note: Wonder ladder: vivid actions (regrow a limb, split into whole worms). Named animals anchor each rung; axolotl and planarian carry the payoff. Keep accuracy: lizard tail regrows as cartilage not bone; starfish whole-body regrowth is species-specific (comet form) — state it precisely. Flag that human-regeneration application is research-in-progress, not an established cure. No overclaiming.

name: Not Dying of Old Age  -  The 'Immortal' Jellyfish
scope: The spine is animals that seem to cheat aging. Rungs: Turritopsis dohrnii, a jellyfish the size of a pinky nail, can — when starved or injured — reverse its life cycle, its adult medusa transforming back into an immature polyp (transdifferentiation) and starting over, in principle without limit, which earns it the nickname 'immortal jellyfish' (though a predator or disease still kills it); the Hydra shows 'negligible senescence' — it doesn't appear to grow measurably more likely to die as it ages, because its body is constantly renewed by stem cells; naked mole-rats barely age and almost never get cancer, staying fertile and healthy for decades; some lobsters keep growing and stay fertile with age. Payoff rung: 'immortal' means it can rewind to a younger stage, NOT that it can't be eaten — the trick is transformation, not invincibility.
source: Britannica; Turritopsis research; Hydra aging studies
framing_note: Named-thing payoff: Turritopsis dohrnii rewinding its own life cycle. Crucial accuracy guard — the final rung must correct the popular myth: 'immortal' = can revert to polyp, still killable by predation/disease. Negligible senescence explained via Hydra as a concrete case, not a bare term. No anthropomorphizing.

name: The Oldest Animals Alive
scope: The spine is extreme lifespan and how we know it. Rungs: the Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate, an estimated ~250-400+ years, meaning some living ones were born before the United States existed — aged by radiocarbon in their slow-growing eye lenses; the ocean quahog clam Ming lived ~507 years, counted by growth rings in its shell like a tree; the bowhead whale can pass 200 years, revealed when old stone harpoon tips were found embedded in living whales; giant tortoises (Aldabra, Galapagos) live past 150 — Jonathan the tortoise is over 190; the rougheye rockfish reaches ~200; the koi and some sturgeon are very long-lived. Payoff rung: a Greenland shark swimming today may have been alive in the 1600s — its age read from the lens of its eye.
source: Britannica; Nielsen et al. Greenland shark aging; ocean quahog studies
framing_note: Wonder = the almost-unbelievable ages, made concrete by HOW we know (eye-lens radiocarbon, shell rings, harpoon tips in living whales). Numbers allowed here because the stem constructs the marvel (born before a nation existed). Named individuals (Ming the clam, Jonathan the tortoise) are coherent hooks whose answer is the animal fact. Flag age ranges as estimates.

name: Living Fast, Dying Young  -  The Mayfly's Single Day
scope: The spine is the opposite extreme — lives compressed into hours or days, and WHY. Rungs: a mayfly spends most of its life (months to years) as an aquatic nymph underwater, then emerges as a winged adult that lives only a day or even hours — the adult has no working mouthparts and cannot eat, its sole job to mate before it dies; whole rivers see mass synchronized hatches so thick they show up on weather radar and pile up like snow; the adult mayfly is the only insect that molts AGAIN after gaining wings (a unique subimago stage); some male honeybee drones die in the act of mating; a gastrotrich lives about three days; the antechinus, a mouse-sized marsupial, has males that mate so frantically for a couple of weeks that their bodies break down and they all die. Payoff rung: the adult mayfly can't eat at all — it has no functioning gut or mouth, because it exists only to reproduce.
source: Britannica; Ephemeroptera biology; entomology refs
framing_note: Wonder = the compressed life and the reason (adult exists only to breed, can't even eat). 'Ephemeroptera' = named-for-a-day is a nice coherent hook. The radar-hatch and the extra-molt subimago are vivid concrete rungs. Keep the nymph-vs-adult ratio accurate (long underwater youth, brief winged adult). No moralizing about death.

name: The Great Migrations
scope: The spine is epic journeys tied to the life cycle, one animal per rung. Rungs: the Arctic tern flies pole to pole and back every year, ~70,000+ km, seeing two summers and more daylight in its life than any animal; the monarch butterfly migration takes MULTIPLE generations — no single butterfly makes the full round trip, yet great-grandchildren return to the same Mexican fir forests their ancestors left, navigating by a sun-compass; the salmon is born in a freshwater stream, lives years at sea, then returns to the EXACT stream it hatched in to spawn, finding it by smell, and Pacific salmon die after spawning; the wildebeest circle the Serengeti in a million-strong herd chasing the rains; the Arctic caribou and the humpback whale run some of the longest mammal migrations; the bar-tailed godwit flies ~13,000 km nonstop across the Pacific without landing, eating, or sleeping normally. Payoff rung: no monarch lives long enough to fly the whole route — the return is completed by a later generation that has never seen the destination.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; monarch & salmon research
framing_note: Named-animal wonders with vivid actions (pole-to-pole, home-stream by smell, multigenerational relay). Strong T1 base: recognize which animal makes which famous journey. The multigenerational monarch relay and the natal-stream salmon return are the payoffs. Godwit nonstop flight is a constructed-number marvel. Keep navigation mechanisms (sun-compass, smell, magnetic sense) factual and flag where still researched.

name: Tool Users
scope: The spine is animals that make and use tools, escalating in cleverness. Rungs: a sea otter carries a favorite rock in a pouch of loose skin under its arm and uses it as an anvil to smash open shellfish on its chest; Egyptian vultures throw stones to crack ostrich eggs; chimpanzees strip a twig to 'fish' termites out of a mound and use stone hammers on nuts; the New Caledonian crow is the standout — it not only uses twigs but MAKES hooks by bending them, keeps favorite tools, and crafts stepped cutting tools from leaves; a captive crow named 007 solved an eight-step puzzle using tools in sequence; some octopuses carry coconut-shell halves to hide inside later — carrying a tool for FUTURE use, rare planning; woodpecker finches use cactus spines to pry out grubs. Payoff rung: the New Caledonian crow doesn't just grab a stick — it manufactures a hooked tool by bending it, and picks the right tool for the job.
source: Britannica; New Caledonian crow research (Hunt, Gray); primatology refs
framing_note: Vivid-action wonders: otter anvil, crow bending a hook, octopus carrying a coconut shelter. Named cases (crow '007') are coherent hooks whose answer is the animal fact. Distinguish tool USE from tool MAKING at higher tiers — the crow's toolmaking is the payoff. Avoid over-anthropomorphizing 'intelligence'; describe the observed behavior. Cite the behavior, not folklore.

name: Recognizing Yourself  -  The Mirror Test
scope: The spine is self-recognition and the famous test for it. Rungs: the mirror mark test puts a dye mark where an animal can only see it in a mirror — if the animal touches the mark ON ITS OWN BODY, it may recognize the reflection as itself, not a rival; great apes (chimpanzees, orangutans, bonobos) pass; so do bottlenose dolphins (they twist to inspect marks), Asian elephants (one touched a mark on its head with its trunk), Eurasian magpies (the first bird to pass, scratching at a colored sticker on its throat), and the cleaner wrasse, a small fish that surprised scientists by trying to scrape off a mark — igniting debate over what 'passing' really means; most animals treat the reflection as another animal — a robin attacks its reflection, a betta flares at it. Payoff rung: a magpie scratching at a sticker only visible in the mirror showed a bird can recognize its own reflection — the first non-mammal to do so.
source: Britannica; Gallup mirror-test literature; magpie & wrasse studies
framing_note: The concrete handle is the mark-and-mirror procedure, not the abstract idea of self-awareness. Named surprises (magpie, cleaner wrasse) carry the wonder. Higher tiers can note the genuine scientific DEBATE over what passing means (the wrasse result is contested) — flag as research-in-progress, present the disagreement neutrally rather than declaring a verdict. Contrast with the robin/betta attacking a rival.

name: Learning a Voice  -  Vocal Mimicry & Learning
scope: The spine is vocal learning — animals that must LEARN their sounds rather than being born knowing them. Rungs: most animals inherit their calls, but a few (songbirds, parrots, hummingbirds, whales, humans) learn them by listening and copying; the lyrebird is the master mimic, reproducing not just other birds but chainsaws, camera shutters, and car alarms it has heard in the forest; parrots can imitate human speech; Alex, an African grey parrot studied for 30 years by Irene Pepperberg, learned ~100 words and could correctly answer questions about the color, shape, and number of objects — his last words to Pepperberg were reportedly 'You be good, I love you'; a beluga whale named Noc lowered his voice to mimic human speech; humpback whale songs spread and change like fashions across an ocean, whole populations updating their tune. Payoff rung: Alex the grey parrot didn't just repeat words — he could answer 'how many?' and 'what color?', showing a parrot can use words meaningfully.
source: Britannica; Pepperberg 'Alex & Me'; lyrebird & humpback song research
framing_note: Alex the parrot is the model coherent hook — the human-drama detail (his last words) is the emotional payoff of a rung whose ANSWER is the animal fact (a parrot answering questions meaningfully). Lyrebird mimicry (chainsaw, camera) is vivid-action wonder. Keep vocal-learning vs innate-call distinction accurate. Don't overclaim animal 'language'; describe what was demonstrated.

name: The Waggle Dance  -  How a Bee Maps the Flowers
scope: The spine is the honeybee's dance language, decoded by Karl von Frisch (Nobel Prize). Rungs: a scout bee that finds good flowers returns to the dark hive and dances on the vertical honeycomb to tell the others where to go; the dance is a figure-eight, and the straight 'waggle' run in the middle carries the message; the ANGLE of the waggle run relative to straight-up encodes the direction to the food relative to the SUN — up means 'fly toward the sun'; the DURATION of the waggle encodes the DISTANCE — a longer waggle means farther away; the bee even corrects for the sun moving across the sky; nearby food gets a simpler 'round dance'; watching bees then fly to the spot confirmed the dance really is read as instructions. Payoff rung: the waggle run is a coded map — its angle points the way relative to the sun, and its length says how far.
source: Britannica; Karl von Frisch dance-language research; apiology refs
framing_note: The wonder is the CODE itself — angle = direction (to the sun), duration = distance. Build it rung by rung so the payoff (reading the map) lands. Von Frisch is a coherent hook (the man who cracked it), not attribution filler. Keep it accurate: sun-referenced angle on a vertical comb, round dance for nearby food. No anthropomorphizing beyond the demonstrated signaling.

name: Making Light  -  Bioluminescence
scope: The spine is living light and what animals DO with it. Rungs: fireflies make cold light in their abdomens with a chemical reaction (luciferin + luciferase + oxygen) and flash in species-specific patterns to find mates — and femme-fatale Photuris females mimic another species' flash to lure and eat the males; the deep-sea anglerfish dangles a glowing lure over its mouth, but it can't make the light itself — the glow comes from BACTERIA living in the lure (a partnership); most deep-sea animals glow, and many use counterillumination — lighting their BELLIES to erase their silhouette against the faint light from above; the Hawaiian bobtail squid hides its shadow with light from bacteria it houses on purpose; the New Zealand glowworm hangs glowing sticky threads from cave ceilings to trap insects; some jellyfish and the dinoflagellate plankton flash blue when disturbed. Payoff rung: the anglerfish doesn't make its own light — glowing bacteria living in its lure do the shining for it.
source: Britannica; MBARI deep-sea bioluminescence research; firefly & bobtail squid studies
framing_note: Wonder-rich: cold chemical light, the femme-fatale firefly, the bacterial partnership in the anglerfish lure, counterillumination that erases a shadow. Each rung one coherent use of light (mate-signal, lure, camouflage, trap). Keep the chemistry named but concrete (luciferin/luciferase). The bacteria-not-self light is the payoff. Cold-light accuracy: almost no heat produced.

name: The Five Vertebrate Classes  -  The Recognition Base
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The backbone family portrait, sorted by the one give-away trait: fish (gills, fins, live in water), amphibians (wet permeable skin, tadpole youth in water — frogs, toads, salamanders, newts), reptiles (dry keratin scales, shelled eggs on land — snakes, lizards, turtles, crocs), birds (feathers — the trait no other living animal has), mammals (fur/hair + milk). Rungs sort a just-harvested creature into its class by its tell: feathers = bird, fur+milk = mammal, dry scales = reptile, wet skin = amphibian, gills = fish. A newt is an amphibian, not a lizard; a whale is a mammal, not a fish; a penguin is a bird under those feathers. Payoff rung: birds ARE living dinosaurs — cladistically nested inside reptiles — so the 'five classes' hides a dinosaur among them.
source: Britannica; AMNH vertebrate overview
framing_note: This is the bank's T1-T2 recognition anchor — carry a heavy recognition floor here. Scene-led: a kid names what they just skinned by its tell, never by memorizing a definition; no 'What is a mammal?' shells. Classic confusers as distractors (newt/lizard, whale/fish, penguin). Keep taxonomy current (birds nested inside reptiles) but state it plainly at the top rung, not as a lecture.

name: What Makes a Mammal
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The hidden signatures every mammal shares: milk (mammary glands — the name-giving trait; 'mammal' from mamma, breast), hair/fur (even a nearly hairless whale has a few bristles as an embryo), warm blood, mostly live birth, and — the invisible tell — three tiny middle-ear bones (malleus, incus, stapes) that no other animal has; a single lower-jaw bone (the dentary). Rungs recognize the signals from outside (fur, feeding young milk) and then the inside secret (three ear bones). Payoff rung: those three middle-ear bones started out as bones at the back of a reptile's JAW, and shifted into the ear over evolution — the fossil record shows the move step by step.
source: Britannica; AMNH; UCMP Berkeley
framing_note: Strong T1 base (fur + milk = mammal). The surprise/payoff is the three-ear-bones signature — invisible from outside, unique to mammals, and evolved from reptile jaw bones (state as standard biology, plainly, no theology). Concrete handle over jargon; introduce malleus/incus/stapes with the image, not as a definition to memorize.

name: What Makes a Bird
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The bird signatures: feathers (the one trait no other living animal has — kept even by flightless ostriches and penguins), toothless beaks, hard-shelled eggs, warm blood, air-filled hollow bones (pneumatic, laced with air sacs) that lighten the skeleton for flight, and a large keeled breastbone anchoring flight muscles. Rungs recognize a bird by feathers first, then the flight-tuned body. Payoff rung: feathers evolved on dinosaurs BEFORE flight (probably for warmth or display), and birds descend from small feathered theropod dinosaurs — a chicken is a closer relative of T. rex than of a crocodile.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; AMNH
framing_note: Feathers = the defining tell, leading every rung (including on flightless birds). Strong T1 recognition base. Scene-led, not 'define bird.' Dinosaur ancestry and feathers-before-flight stated as standard biology. The chicken/T. rex kinship is the wonder payoff — keep it accurate (theropod lineage).

name: What Makes a Reptile / an Amphibian  -  Dry Scales vs Wet Skin
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The two classes side by side. Reptiles: dry, waterproof keratin scales; amniotic shelled eggs laid on land (or live birth) that freed them from water; ectothermic (bask to warm up); snakes, lizards, turtles, crocodiles. Amphibians: smooth, moist, permeable skin they can breathe THROUGH (so they must stay damp and are sensitive to pollution); eggs laid in water with no shell; a two-stage life — a water-breathing larva (tadpole) that metamorphoses into the adult; frogs, toads, salamanders, newts, caecilians. Rungs give the tell: touch it — a snake is dry, a frog is wet. Payoff rung: the amphibian's skin is a working lung — it swaps oxygen right through the skin, which is why it must stay moist and why it can't live in the sea.
source: Britannica; AmphibiaWeb; AMNH
framing_note: Dry-vs-wet skin is the memorable handle and a good T1-T2 recognition rung. Scene-led (touch the harvested animal). The shelled-egg-on-land vs egg-in-water contrast is the deeper why. Distractors confuse newt/salamander (amphibian) with lizard (reptile). Don't lean on 'cold-blooded' as the only frame — pair with ectotherm at T3. Skin-breathing is the amphibian payoff.

name: The Big Invertebrate Groups
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The major invertebrate phyla by their body-plan tell — invertebrates are ~95% of all animal species. Rungs: arthropods (jointed legs + external skeleton — insects, spiders, crabs; the biggest group by far); mollusks (soft body, often a shell, a muscular foot — snails, clams, octopuses); cnidarians (stinging cells, radial bodies, one opening — jellyfish, corals, anemones); echinoderms (five-fold symmetry, tube feet, water-vascular system — starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers); annelids/worms (segmented ringed bodies — earthworms, leeches); sponges (no true tissues, just filter-feeding pores). Rungs sort a creature by its plan: jointed legs = arthropod, stinging tentacles = cnidarian, five arms = echinoderm. Payoff rung: an octopus and a snail are cousins — both mollusks — even though one is a genius hunter and the other carries a shell on its back.
source: Britannica; AMNH invertebrate zoology; Brusca Invertebrates
framing_note: A second T1-T2 recognition anchor (paired with the vertebrate classes). Scene-led sorting by the give-away trait, never a bare phylum definition. The octopus/snail-are-cousins and starfish-five-fold-symmetry facts are the wonder hooks. Keep current phylum names and the arthropod-dominance fact accurate. Distractors mix the phyla (jellyfish vs starfish, crab vs snail).

name: Radial vs Bilateral  -  Why a Jellyfish Has No Front
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The spine is the two great body symmetries. Rungs: a jellyfish, sea anemone, or starfish is RADIALLY symmetric — built like a wheel around a center, no front or back, so it can meet food or danger coming from any direction (good for a drifter or a sit-and-wait animal); almost every active, moving animal — including you, a fish, an insect, a worm — is BILATERALLY symmetric, with a mirror-image left and right, a definite FRONT and back; having a front let the sense organs and mouth cluster there and a brain form to process what's ahead — this is called cephalization (a head end); a starfish is the odd case — its larva is bilateral, and it evolved five-fold radial symmetry LATER as an adult. Payoff rung: having a front and back is why animals evolved a HEAD — sense organs and a brain gathered at the leading end, where the action is.
source: Britannica; AMNH; developmental biology refs
framing_note: The wonder is the payoff logic: a front end drives having a head (cephalization). Scene-led with named animals (jellyfish = no front; you = a front). Radial-suits-a-drifter vs bilateral-suits-a-mover is the concrete why. The starfish-was-bilateral-first twist is a good higher rung. Teach cephalization via the image (senses gather at the front), not as a bare term.

name: Growing by Molting  -  The Exoskeleton Problem
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The spine is the trade-off of wearing your skeleton on the outside. Rungs: arthropods (insects, crabs, spiders) have a hard external shell (exoskeleton) of chitin that protects them and anchors muscles — but it can't stretch, so to grow the animal must SHED the whole suit and swell into a new, soft one before it hardens (molting/ecdysis); a freshly molted crab or cicada is pale and helpless until the new shell hardens, so it hides; a cicada nymph climbs a tree, splits its back, and crawls out leaving a ghost-shell clinging to the bark; a spider molts to grow and can even regrow a lost leg at a molt; a lobster molts dozens of times as it grows; molting animals (arthropods + roundworms + others) form a whole group called Ecdysozoa named for this shedding. Payoff rung: an arthropod can't just get bigger inside its shell — it must climb out of its old skeleton entirely and grow a new one, defenseless until it hardens.
source: Britannica; AMNH; entomology & carcinology refs
framing_note: Concrete wonder: the empty cicada shell on the bark, the soft helpless newly-molted crab. The core insight is WHY they molt — a rigid outside skeleton can't grow with them. Scene-led. Introduce exoskeleton/chitin/molting via the image. The defenseless-after-molt vulnerability is a coherent rung (and a real predation window). Keep Ecdysozoa mention light, only at the top tier.

name: The Rule-Breakers  -  Monotremes & Marsupials
strand: Body plans & the tree of life
scope: The spine is mammals that break the 'live birth + nipples' rule. Rungs: monotremes are the only mammals that LAY EGGS yet still make milk — just five living species: the platypus and four echidnas; they have no nipples, so milk oozes out through patches of skin and the babies lap it up; the platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) piles on more oddities — a duck-like bill that senses the faint electricity of prey, webbed feet, and a venomous spur on the male's hind leg; marsupials give birth to a tiny, jellybean-sized, half-formed newborn that crawls unaided up the mother's fur into a POUCH, latches onto a nipple, and finishes developing there — a kangaroo joey is born the size of a bean; koalas, wombats, opossums, and Tasmanian devils are marsupials; a wombat's pouch faces BACKWARD so digging doesn't fill it with dirt. Payoff rung: the platypus lays eggs, has no nipples, hunts by electricity through its bill, and the male carries venom — a mammal that breaks nearly every rule.
source: Britannica; Australian Museum; AMNH
framing_note: Wonder-led rule-breaking: the platypus mash-up (bill, spur, eggs, milk-through-skin) and the bean-sized joey crawling to the pouch. Real binomial Ornithorhynchus anatinus if named. EXACTLY five living monotreme species — state precisely. Backward-facing wombat pouch is a great coherent rung. No anthropomorphizing; keep the milk-through-skin and electroreception facts accurate.
